new_elements: Temperature-target dial function (Replaces power levels with targets like warm, hot, and boiling.)
rationale: Everyday words replace technical power settings, reducing learning.
judge_comment: Everyday words are friendlier than power levels, but a dial still has to be learned and this is a modest change rather than a radical one.

title: Pictogram presets
new_elements: Pictogram preset function (Replaces multi-step settings with large pictograms for popcorn, pizza, and reheat.)
rationale: One-tap pictures guide users without any manual.
judge_comment: One-tap pictograms are intuitive and easy to build, but many microwaves already offer similar presets.

title: RFID recipe tag
new_elements: RFID recipe tag function (Replaces timer and power knobs with tags attached to meal containers.)
rationale: Users just place the tagged meal in and close the door.
judge_comment: Place the tagged meal and close the door, with no controls to learn, though it needs tagged containers and an ecosystem.

title: NFC tap-to-cook
new_elements: NFC tap-to-cook function (Replaces control panel with tap-to-cook from a phone or smart package.)
rationale: A single familiar tap replaces all microwave-specific controls.
judge_comment: NFC is feasible and familiar, but it depends on a phone and smart packaging, and it adds a dependency instead of simplifying.

title: Gesture control
new_elements: Gesture control function (Replaces knobs and buttons with simple swipe and point gestures.)
rationale: Gestures are natural and require no button memorization.
judge_comment: Gestures sound natural, but they are not discoverable, can misfire, and may demand more learning than buttons.

title: Door-close auto-start
new_elements: Door-close auto-start function (Replaces start button with automatic start when the door closes.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only action needed to begin cooking.
judge_comment: Auto-start on door close removes a step, but it risks accidental heating of an empty or unintended load, and it is not very radical.

title: One-button stop
new_elements: One-button stop function (Replaces multiple cancellation steps with a single large stop button.)
rationale: Stopping is always obvious and never requires resetting learned modes.
judge_comment: A big stop button is helpful but is already standard, and it addresses only cancellation, not operation.

title: Large rotary dial only
new_elements: Large rotary dial only function (Replaces all buttons and displays with one oversized dial.)
rationale: A single tactile control is universally understood and easy to use.
judge_comment: A single oversized dial is intuitive and strongly serves the no-learning-curve need, though similar mechanical-dial microwaves already exist.

title: No-display color progress
new_elements: No-display color progress function (Replaces numeric timer readout with a color-changing rim.)
rationale: Users can see cooking progress without reading numbers or settings.
judge_comment: A color-changing rim is a fresh way to show progress without numbers, but it conveys little precise information.

title: LED ring status
new_elements: LED ring status function (Replaces interior lamp and bell with an exterior LED ring that shows done and running states.)
rationale: Status is visible from across the room with no controls to interpret.
judge_comment: An exterior LED ring shows status from a distance, but it mainly aids feedback rather than operation, and removing the interior lamp hurts usability.

title: Camera auto-recognition
new_elements: Camera auto-recognition function (Replaces manual settings with a camera that identifies food and cooks it.)
rationale: The microwave makes all decisions, so the user does nothing but place food.
judge_comment: Camera food recognition removes all settings and directly serves zero-learning use, though it already exists in some premium ovens and is not a cheaper substitution.

title: Projected cooking guide
new_elements: Projected cooking guide function (Replaces printed labels with light projected directly onto the food area.)
rationale: Guidance appears where the user is already looking, removing label learning.
judge_comment: Projected guidance is intuitive and novel, but it still requires the user to follow instructions and adds cost and complexity.

title: Self-stirring bowl
new_elements: Self-stirring bowl function (Replaces turntable and manual stirring with a bowl that stirs food internally.)
rationale: Users do not need to set turntable or pause to stir.
judge_comment: A self-stirring bowl is wild and removes stirring, but it is mechanically hard, needs special cookware, and is vague about how it works.

title: Stationary waveguide stirrer
new_elements: Stationary waveguide stirrer function (Replaces the rotating glass turntable with a fixed microwave stirrer.)
rationale: No turntable to align, remove, or clean makes operation simpler.
judge_comment: Stirrer-based flatbed microwaves already exist and are cheap and feasible, but they only marginally improve operation simplicity.

title: Rotating antenna
new_elements: Rotating antenna function (Replaces turntable motor with a rotating microwave antenna.)
rationale: Even heating happens without the user placing food on a turntable.
judge_comment: A rotating antenna is a proven design that removes the turntable, but it is not very radical and the user benefit is modest.

title: Vibrating plate
new_elements: Vibrating plate function (Replaces turntable with a flat plate that gently vibrates food for even heating.)
rationale: A flat surface is easier to load and requires no turntable positioning.
judge_comment: Vibrating plate is a plausible turntable substitute but does little to simplify operation, and vibrating liquids or food would be messy and add its own complexity.

title: Disposable rotating liner
new_elements: Disposable rotating liner function (Replaces permanent turntable with a disposable liner that rotates or stirs.)
rationale: No cleaning or turntable handling means less learning and effort.
judge_comment: A disposable liner reduces cleaning but adds consumables, and the rotating mechanism is unclear, so it barely addresses the learning curve.

title: Thermally insulated pod
new_elements: Thermally insulated pod function (Replaces open cavity with a sealed pod that cooks preset meals.)
rationale: Users insert a pod and press one button, avoiding all settings.
judge_comment: Pods with one-button cooking strongly eliminate settings and are technically feasible, though the concept resembles existing pod and barcode cooking products.

title: Phase-array no-door containment
new_elements: Phase-array no-door containment function (Replaces the door and latch with a field that contains microwaves.)
rationale: No door to open or close makes the microwave as simple as a bowl.
judge_comment: Doorless containment is highly radical but physically implausible and unsafe, and removing the door barely reduces learning.

title: Smart absorbing material
new_elements: Smart absorbing material function (Replaces power knob with cavity material that absorbs excess microwave energy.)
rationale: Users cannot overcook as easily and never need to set power.
judge_comment: Self-limiting absorbing material would remove power settings and overcooking, but how it would work without wasting the energy needed to heat the food is unclear.

title: USB-C simple power
new_elements: USB-C simple power function (Replaces 230 V plug and complex supply with a universal USB-C power input.)
rationale: A familiar phone-charger plug removes fear of electrical setup.
judge_comment: A microwave draws about 1,000+ W, which USB-C cannot supply, and the plug is not what makes operation hard, so it barely serves the need.

title: Shape-memory timer
new_elements: Shape-memory timer function (Replaces clockwork timer with a shape-memory alloy that simply pops when done.)
rationale: A physical pop signal is intuitive and needs no clock reading.
judge_comment: A shape-memory alloy pop is an unusual physical cue that needs no clock reading, though setting the duration and heating the alloy reliably is unclear.

title: Ambient light window
new_elements: Ambient light window function (Replaces interior lamp with a window that uses room light.)
rationale: No lamp control or bulb knowledge is needed to see inside.
judge_comment: It is feasible and removes a lamp, but it only marginally helps operation and room light would give poor visibility inside.

title: Steam sensor cut-off
new_elements: Steam sensor cut-off function (Replaces timer with a sensor that turns off at the first strong steam burst.)
rationale: Users can reheat without choosing any time.
judge_comment: Steam-sensor auto cut-off already exists in sensor-reheat modes, but it directly removes time selection and fits the no-learning-curve goal well.

title: Popcorn button only
new_elements: Popcorn button only function (Replaces full control panel with a single popcorn button for the most common snack.)
rationale: One labeled button is instantly understandable and needs no learning curve.
judge_comment: One button is very easy to understand and simple to build, but it is limited to one use and not very radical.

title: Pizza button only
new_elements: Pizza button only function (Replaces multi-setting panel with one pizza reheat button.)
rationale: A single recognizable action avoids any power or time decisions.
judge_comment: Very simple but too narrow, since a pizza-only microwave fails most other tasks, and it is not very radical.

title: Reheat button only
new_elements: Reheat button only function (Replaces all controls with one reheat button using adaptive sensing.)
rationale: The most common microwave task becomes a single obvious press.
judge_comment: A single adaptive reheat button strongly meets the zero-learning need, and sensor-based reheat already exists, but it is still plausible and useful.

title: Defrost-by-weight
new_elements: Defrost-by-weight function (Replaces manual defrost power cycling with automatic weight-based defrost.)
rationale: Users do not need to learn defrost times or turning instructions.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto defrost removes a confusing task and exists in many products, though it adds little radical change.

title: Keep-warm until opened
new_elements: Keep-warm until opened function (Replaces bell and hold settings with automatic keep-warm after cooking.)
rationale: No need to rush or understand keep-warm modes.
judge_comment: Auto keep-warm eases the end of cooking but does not address starting or operating the microwave.

title: Child-proof single knob
new_elements: Child-proof single knob function (Replaces complex child-lock sequences with a knob that only turns after a simple press.)
rationale: Safety is built into one intuitive motion, not a learned button code.
judge_comment: A press-then-turn knob simplifies the child lock and is concrete, but it addresses only safety rather than core operation.

title: Voice feedback
new_elements: Voice feedback function (Replaces display messages with spoken confirmations like cooking and done.)
rationale: Users hear what is happening without reading or interpreting icons.
judge_comment: Spoken confirmations are easy and mildly helpful, but they do not simplify input and voice feedback is not radical.

title: Haptic knob feedback
new_elements: Haptic knob feedback function (Replaces numeric markings with vibration stops for time and power.)
rationale: The knob tells users when they reach useful settings, reducing learning.
judge_comment: A knob with haptic detents replaces numeric markings and guides users intuitively, though the mechanism is only moderately detailed.

title: Self-cleaning steam
new_elements: Self-cleaning steam function (Replaces manual cleaning routines with a one-button steam clean cycle.)
rationale: Maintenance becomes a single action rather than a learned procedure.
judge_comment: One-button steam cleaning is about maintenance, not operating the microwave, so it only weakly addresses the need.

title: Automatic door opening
new_elements: Automatic door opening function (Replaces push-release button with a door that opens automatically when done.)
rationale: Users do not need to press or find a release button.
judge_comment: An auto-opening door removes one small step, but it barely affects the learning curve and has safety and cost trade-offs.

title: AI meal pod recognition
new_elements: AI meal pod recognition function (Replaces all controls with a system that recognizes branded meal pods and cooks them.)
rationale: The user only inserts the pod, so there is nothing to learn or set.
judge_comment: Pod insertion removes all settings, so there is truly nothing to learn, but it locks users into branded pods and needs recognition infrastructure.

title: One-Touch Cook Button
new_elements: One-touch cook button (Single start control that selects a safe default time and power.); Auto-selects cooking profile (Infers time and power without user input.)
rationale: One press replaces two knob settings, eliminating learning curve.
judge_comment: Already common (Quick Start buttons); a safe default time/power is vague and not radical, though it does simplify operation.

title: Humidity-Sensing Auto Power
new_elements: Humidity sensor auto-power (Detects steam and adjusts duty cycle automatically.); Auto-adjusts power (Replaces manual 5-step power knob.)
rationale: Users never choose a power level; the microwave senses and decides.
judge_comment: Sensor cooking exists in premium models, but it concretely replaces the power knob with a named mechanism and removes the decision.

title: Single Less/More Dial
new_elements: Less/more dial (One dial nudges an auto profile instead of setting time and power.)
rationale: A single relative control removes numeric settings and labels.
judge_comment: A single relative dial is intuitive and somewhat fresh, but the underlying auto profile is undefined.

title: Touch-Anywhere Open
new_elements: Capacitive door-open strip (Touching anywhere along the door edge releases the latch.); Touch-to-release latch (Capacitive sensing drives the latch actuator.)
rationale: No button to find or press; any touch opens the door.
judge_comment: Novel and concrete, but it only addresses door opening, risks accidental opening, and leaves the cooking operation unchanged.

title: Voice-Only Cook
new_elements: Voice command microwave (Listens for simple words like cook, stop, and done.); Listens for cook/done (Maps spoken intent to a safe default cycle.)
rationale: Speaking is a universal interface with almost no learning curve.
judge_comment: Voice control is an existing feature, and the default cycle is vague, but it needs almost no learning.

title: Wave-to-Start Gesture
new_elements: IR gesture sensor (Detects a hand wave across the front panel.); Starts default reheat (Gesture triggers a single safe reheat cycle.)
rationale: A wave starts cooking without touching or reading controls.
judge_comment: A touchless wave start is simple to use, but accidental triggering is a safety concern and it substitutes only the start button.

title: Scan-to-Cook
new_elements: Barcode/QR scanner (Reads package instructions and sets the cycle.); Sets exact cook from package (Eliminates manual time and power entry.)
rationale: The user scans and walks away; no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Scanning package codes removes manual entry, but it depends on barcode and cooking-instruction databases and fails for unpackaged food.

title: Reheat-Only Button
new_elements: Reheat button (Only one cooking button on the entire panel.); Fixed safe reheat cycle (Uses a conservative default profile.)
rationale: A single obvious button means there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single button is the simplest possible interface and very feasible, but it is not radical and limits cooking flexibility.

title: Weight-Sensing Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Weighs food as it is placed in the cavity.); Auto time by weight (Sets cooking time from weight alone.)
rationale: Users just put food in; no time or power decisions.
judge_comment: A load cell is a concrete, plausible sensor, but weight alone is a poor proxy for cook time and the turntable is hard to instrument.

title: No Turntable, Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Mode stirrer (Rotating metal paddle distributes microwaves without a turntable.); Even heating without plate alignment (Removes the need to center or orient a plate.)
rationale: Removing the turntable removes a positioning step from operation.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already common and the benefit to operation is marginal, since users still must set time and power.

title: Flat Ceramic Floor with Stirrer
new_elements: Flat ceramic cavity floor (No rotating glass plate to align or clean.); Rotating antenna stirrer (Hidden antenna moves the microwave pattern.)
rationale: A flat floor is instantly intuitive and requires no placement skill.
judge_comment: Flat-floor microwaves with stirrers already exist and are easy to use, but they have little effect on operating complexity.

title: Lamp-Free Transparent Window
new_elements: UV-stable transparent door panel (See-through door needs no interior lamp.); See inside without interior lamp (Ambient light reveals the food.)
rationale: No lamp switch or bulb means one less thing to understand.
judge_comment: Relying on ambient light is unreliable, especially in a dark kitchen, and it barely helps usability.

title: Door-Edge LED Glow
new_elements: Door-edge LED strip (Lights the cavity only when the door opens.); Lights cavity automatically (No separate light switch or control.)
rationale: The light simply behaves as expected when the door opens.
judge_comment: Automatic door lighting is already standard, and it adds little to the target need.

title: Magnetic Self-Closing Door
new_elements: Magnetic self-latch (Magnets pull the door closed and align the seal.); Push-to-open magnetic door (A light push releases the door.)
rationale: The door closes and opens intuitively without a button or latch handle.
judge_comment: A push-to-open, self-closing magnetic door is a plausible convenience, but it only touches door handling and not operating the controls.

title: Magnetic Interlock Sensor
new_elements: Hall-effect interlock (Senses door position magnetically with fewer moving switches.); Senses door closed (Enables cooking only when the door is shut.)
rationale: Hidden automatic safety removes user awareness from the task.
judge_comment: The safety interlock is hidden from the user and does nothing to remove the learning curve.

title: Capacitive Timer Slider
new_elements: Capacitive touch slider (One-finger time nudge with no numbers to interpret.); One-finger time nudge (Slide right to add time, left to reduce.)
rationale: A directional slider is self-explanatory compared to a mechanical timer.
judge_comment: A slider is intuitive and feasible, but it only simplifies time entry and is not radical.

title: Preset Food Icons
new_elements: Food icon buttons (Picture buttons for popcorn, pizza, beverage, leftovers.); Maps icon to auto cook (Each icon runs a safe preset.)
rationale: Pictures replace words and numbers, reducing learning to near zero.
judge_comment: Icon presets are very easy to use but are already common on microwaves.

title: Single Popcorn Memory
new_elements: Popcorn button (One dedicated button for the most common snack.); Fixed popcorn profile (Uses time and power preset for popcorn.)
rationale: The user presses the only button they recognize for the task.
judge_comment: A popcorn button is long-established and covers only one task.

title: Auto-Defrost Only
new_elements: Auto-defrost button (Single button for thawing frozen food.); Weight-free defrost cycle (Pulsing low-power cycle safe for most frozen foods.)
rationale: No weight entry or power selection is needed to defrost.
judge_comment: A one-button defrost is simple, but a weight-free cycle may thaw unevenly and covers a narrow use.

title: Child-Simple Start/Stop
new_elements: Start/stop single toggle (One large toggle starts or stops cooking.); One action starts and stops (No separate cancel or reset control.)
rationale: One physical control with two states is immediately understandable.
judge_comment: A single start/stop control is clear and easy to build, but it is a basic simplification.

title: Kill Power Knob
new_elements: Continuous full-power only (Microwave always runs at full power.); No power selector (Removes the 5-step power knob entirely.)
rationale: Eliminating power choice removes a whole decision from operation.
judge_comment: Removing power choice simplifies operation and is trivially feasible, though full-power-only harms results for defrosting and delicate foods and it isn't very radical.

title: Timer as Sandglass
new_elements: Mechanical sand timer visual (Shows remaining time as falling sand rather than numbers.); Visual countdown without numbers (Sand level maps directly to time remaining.)
rationale: Reading time becomes as intuitive as watching sand fall.
judge_comment: A sand timer is intuitive to read, but a mechanical one must be set and calibrated to variable cook times and doesn't clearly simplify operation.

title: Color-Coded Time Ring
new_elements: Color-changing time ring (Ring changes color as time counts down.); Shows done without reading (Color shift signals completion.)
rationale: Color feedback removes the need to read or interpret a timer.
judge_comment: A color ring is easy to build and offers glanceable feedback, but input is still needed and the color meaning may have to be learned.

title: Bell Replaced by Light Pulse
new_elements: Done light halo (Soft pulsing light signals completion.); Signals completion visually (No audible bell to understand or silence.)
rationale: A visible glow is self-evident and does not require learning a bell.
judge_comment: A light pulse is simple and feasible, but it only addresses the completion signal, not operation, and can be missed when out of sight.

title: Bell Replaced by Fragrance Burst
new_elements: Aroma release capsule (Releases a food-like scent when cooking finishes.); Smell signals done (Completion is communicated by scent.)
rationale: Smell is an ancient, zero-learning completion cue.
judge_comment: A scent cue is highly novel and intuitive, but capsules are consumable, unreliable and impractical, and it doesn't simplify operation much.

title: Bleeder Resistor HV Discharge
new_elements: Integrated bleeder resistor (Automatically drains high voltage after switch-off.); Auto-discharges HV (No user or service action required.)
rationale: A hidden automatic safety function removes a dangerous concept from operation.
judge_comment: Bleeder resistors already exist in microwaves and have nothing to do with ease of operation, so it is neither radical nor relevant.

title: Self-Resetting Thermal Fuse
new_elements: PTC self-reset protector (Cuts power on overheat and resets when cool.); Protects overheat without reset (No user reset procedure.)
rationale: Users never encounter a reset step after an overheat event.
judge_comment: Thermal fuses and PTC resets are standard, and the user rarely meets a reset step anyway, so it barely helps the learning curve.

title: Metal-Detect Auto Cutoff
new_elements: Metal detector in cavity (Senses metal before arcing starts.); Stops arcing before user notices (Cuts power and signals safely.)
rationale: The microwave handles a dangerous mistake automatically, so users need not learn rules.
judge_comment: Automatic metal detection removes a rule users would otherwise have to learn, though reliable sensing in a cavity is hard and it isn't a substitution.

title: Auto-Stir Pulse for Superheat
new_elements: Pulse-stir heating (Interrupts heating to prevent superheated liquids.); Steam burst agitation (Small steam bursts break surface tension.)
rationale: Safe heating happens without users learning about superheating.
judge_comment: Pulsed heating that prevents superheating without user knowledge is plausible and useful, but it targets a narrow case and the steam-burst mechanism is vague.

title: Anti-Superheat Lid Sensor
new_elements: Lid presence sensor (Detects a loose lid or stirring stick.); Warns if no stirring stick (Simple icon tells user to add a stick.)
rationale: The microwave teaches the safe habit with one clear signal.
judge_comment: A lid or stick sensor with an icon is feasible, but it adds a warning the user must understand and falls short of zero learning.

title: One-Button Crisp
new_elements: Susceptor-lined auto pan (A pan with microwave-active coating browns food.); Crisp mode one press (Single button runs a crisp cycle.)
rationale: Browning becomes an automatic preset rather than a learned technique.
judge_comment: Susceptor pans exist and a one-press crisp cycle is plausible, but it mainly simplifies browning rather than the overall operation, and it is not very radical.

title: Browning Pan Ejector
new_elements: Pop-up crisp tray (Tray rises when crisp mode is selected.); Adds browning without settings (Tray position and time are automatic.)
rationale: Users get crisping without understanding susceptors or power levels.
judge_comment: A pop-up crisp tray is a more novel mechanism, but it adds mechanical complexity and cost inside the cavity, which sits poorly with the substitution brief.

title: No-Door-Button Push Panel
new_elements: Push-anywhere door panel (Pressing anywhere on the door opens it.); Flexure latch (Flexible hinge and latch release with a push.)
rationale: No specific button location to learn; any push works.
judge_comment: A push-anywhere door with a flexure latch replaces the button with something simpler and cheaper, though opening the door was never the hard part.

title: Foot Pedal Open
new_elements: Foot pedal door release (A pedal opens the door hands-free.); Hands-free opening (Works when hands are full.)
rationale: A pedal is an obvious physical control with no interface learning.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is intuitive and works hands-free, but it is awkward for a countertop microwave and does not address operating complexity.

title: Proximity Wake Panel
new_elements: Proximity wake (Panel wakes and defaults when a person approaches.); Panel lights and defaults ready (No need to press wake or select mode.)
rationale: The microwave anticipates use and presents only a default action.
judge_comment: Proximity wake with a default-ready panel directly cuts the steps needed to start, though it is not a true substitution of parts and defaults may not suit every food.

title: Default 30-Second Nudge
new_elements: +30s button (Adds thirty seconds with one press.); Adds time with one press (No time setting needed for common tasks.)
rationale: The most common action is one press, not a timed dial adjustment.
judge_comment: Already common on real microwaves, so highly feasible and helpful but not radical.

title: Default 1-Minute Start
new_elements: Fixed one-minute cycle (Starts a safe one-minute full-power cycle.); Minute button (One button labeled one minute.)
rationale: A fixed one-minute button is immediately usable without setting time.
judge_comment: Simple and usable, but a fixed minute fits few tasks and isn't very novel.

title: No Clock Display
new_elements: Blank minimalist panel (No clock, no numbers, only one start control.); Removes clock setting (Eliminates a common setup task.)
rationale: Removing the clock removes the first learning obstacle for many users.
judge_comment: Removing the clock cuts a setup step, but a single start control with no time input limits function.

title: Auto-Off When Door Opens
new_elements: Door-open auto-stop (Cooking stops immediately when door opens.); Door switch direct cutoff (Mechanical switch cuts magnetron power.)
rationale: Users can always stop by opening the door, a natural expected action.
judge_comment: Door interlocks already exist as standard safety; it helps stopping but not the operation learning curve much.

title: Single Motion Dial
new_elements: Spring-return dial (Turn and release starts a timed cook.); Turn and release starts timed cook (Time maps directly to dial rotation.)
rationale: One physical motion both sets and starts, with no separate start button.
judge_comment: A spring-return dial that sets and starts in one motion is intuitive, simple, and a genuine substitution of buttons.

title: Mechanical Timer with Detents
new_elements: Detented timer dial (Dial clicks at one-minute intervals.); 1-min clicks (Mechanical detents make short times repeatable.)
rationale: Click stops remove the guesswork of an imprecise mechanical timer.
judge_comment: Mechanical dial timers already exist, but detents give a simple, intuitive interface with no learning curve; it is a minor tweak, not a radical idea.

title: Digital Timer with One Button
new_elements: One-button digital timer (Press cycles through 30s, 1m, 2m, 5m.); Press cycles preset times (No numeric keypad or clock setting.)
rationale: Cycling preset times is simpler than learning a keypad or dial scale.
judge_comment: A one-button preset cycler is very simple to use and easy to build, though it limits flexibility and is not especially novel.

title: Power Knob Replaced by Food Sensor
new_elements: Infrared food sensor (Measures surface temperature and doneness.); Auto selects power (Sensor chooses duty cycle.)
rationale: No power levels to learn; the microwave senses the food itself.
judge_comment: Sensor-driven automatic power directly removes the need to learn settings, but IR measures only surface temperature, so reliability is limited, and similar sensors already exist.

title: Interlock by Reed Switch
new_elements: Reed switch (Magnetic reed switch senses door position.); Door position sensing (Simple on/off signal for safety.)
rationale: A sealed magnetic switch reduces mechanical complexity and user awareness.
judge_comment: Reed switch interlocks are a hidden internal part change and do little to make the product easier to operate.

title: Door Choke Replaced by Conductive Gasket
new_elements: Conductive elastomer gasket (Soft gasket seals RF without precise choke geometry.); RF seal without precise choke (Allows easier, more forgiving door closing.)
rationale: The door can be closed casually without aligning a precision choke.
judge_comment: A conductive gasket could make door closing more forgiving, but it barely affects operation, and RF leakage and wear are real concerns.

title: HV Diode Replaced by SiC Module
new_elements: SiC HV rectifier module (Combines rectifier and voltage doubler in one package.); Simpler fewer parts (Reduces internal complexity and failure points.)
rationale: Fewer internal parts means more reliable operation with no user intervention.
judge_comment: An internal component swap that users never see, so it does nothing for learning curve, and it is not radical.

title: Turntable Motor Replaced by Magnetic Stirrer
new_elements: Magnetic cavity stirrer (Hidden magnetic paddle stirs the microwave field.); No turntable alignment (Food does not need to be centered.)
rationale: Removing the visible turntable removes a placement and cleaning step.
judge_comment: Stirrers already exist in microwaves, and removing the turntable cuts one placement concern, though a magnetic paddle is a vague mechanism.

title: Bell Replaced by Phone Notification
new_elements: Bluetooth completion alert (Sends a notification to the user's phone.); Sends done to phone (Completion message appears on phone.)
rationale: The user already understands phone notifications, so no new signal to learn.
judge_comment: Feasible and familiar, but it adds pairing setup and doesn't simplify core operation.

title: Mains Cord Replaced by Inductive Base
new_elements: Inductive power base (Microwave sits on a powered base with no plug.); Drop microwave on base, no plug (Power transfers wirelessly.)
rationale: No cord or plug orientation makes setup and repositioning trivial.
judge_comment: Wireless power at microwave-level wattage is impractical and it only affects setup, not operation.

title: Door Button Replaced by Kick-to-Open
new_elements: Kick sensor (A tap with foot or knee opens the door.); Opens door with tap (No hands and no button location to learn.)
rationale: Any tap opens the door, making operation obvious and hands-free.
judge_comment: Kick-to-open is hands-free and easy to grasp, though accidental triggering is a risk and it doesn't address the controls.

title: One-Button Cook
new_elements: SingleCookButton (One large button replaces timer and power knobs.); AutoCookCycle (Runs a safe default heating cycle automatically.)
rationale: One press replaces all power and time decisions, so there is no learning curve.
judge_comment: Very simple and workable, but it's an obvious, existing concept and a single default cycle may not suit all foods.

title: Any-Food AutoSense
new_elements: MultiSensorArray (Cheap sensors detect moisture, weight, and temperature.); AutoDetectCook (Infers food type and cooks it without user input.)
rationale: Sensors decide time and power, removing every setting from the user.
judge_comment: Removes all settings and truly zero-learning, though reliable food inference with cheap sensors is hard and the idea is not very new.

title: Door-Close Start
new_elements: DoorSensor (Detects when the door is fully closed.); AutoStartOnClose (Begins cooking as soon as the door closes.)
rationale: Closing the door starts cooking, so no separate start control is needed.
judge_comment: Eliminates the start step and is easy to build, but auto-starting raises safety and duration questions and doesn't define what is cooked.

title: Voice 'Cook'
new_elements: VoiceModule (Low-cost microphone and command chip.); VoiceCookCommand (Responds to a single spoken word.)
rationale: Saying one word replaces dials and buttons entirely.
judge_comment: Voice control exists already, and it still needs time or power input, plus it can misfire in noisy kitchens.

title: Tap-to-Cook NFC
new_elements: NFCReader (Reads a phone or sticker tap.); TapRecipeCook (Loads and runs a cooking preset from a tap.)
rationale: Tapping a phone or tag sets cooking automatically with no programming.
judge_comment: NFC presets are feasible but need a phone or tags, adding setup and learning that works against the no-learning-curve goal.

title: Package Barcode Scan
new_elements: BarcodeScanner (Scans standard food package barcodes.); ScanAndCook (Uses package instructions to set the cycle.)
rationale: Scanning a package removes manual interpretation of cooking instructions.
judge_comment: Barcodes don't encode cooking instructions, so it needs a database lookup, but scanning would remove the need to interpret package directions.

title: QR Meal Scan
new_elements: QRScanner (Reads QR codes printed on meal packaging.); QRPresetCook (Runs the exact cook cycle encoded in the QR code.)
rationale: QR code carries the correct settings, so the user does nothing but scan.
judge_comment: Feasible and simple for the user, though it only works with packaging that carries the code and has been done in part by some brands.

title: Weight-Only Dial
new_elements: WeightSensor (Measures food weight on the base.); WeightAutoTime (Sets time from weight and food category.)
rationale: Placing food and closing the door is enough because weight sets time.
judge_comment: Weight sensing is easy to build, but the food category still has to be chosen, so the learning curve isn't fully removed.

title: Steam-Sensor Stop
new_elements: SteamSensor (Detects moisture released by hot food.); SteamStop (Stops cooking when steam indicates doneness.)
rationale: Microwave stops by itself, so the user does not need timer knowledge.
judge_comment: Sensor-cook is already common in microwaves, but it fits the need well, with place, close, and done.

title: Thermal-Camera Stop
new_elements: ThermalCamera (Cheap infrared array watches surface temperature.); ThermalAutoStop (Stops heating at a safe target temperature.)
rationale: It watches temperature and stops by itself, eliminating guessing.
judge_comment: A low-cost IR array that stops at a target temperature gives true hands-off cooking, though accuracy and the lack of a food-specific target remain open problems.

title: Food-Camera Preset
new_elements: FoodCamera (Low-resolution camera recognizes common foods.); VisualFoodPreset (Chooses settings from a visual match.)
rationale: Camera recognizes food and picks settings automatically with no input.
judge_comment: Camera-based food recognition removes all input, though it adds cost and accuracy limits, and it's more complex than a simple substitution.

title: Pictogram Dial
new_elements: PictogramDial (Dial face uses only food icons, no numbers or words.); IconOnlySelect (Selects a preset by pointing at an icon.)
rationale: Icons replace numbers and words for zero-reading operation.
judge_comment: Icon-only dial is simple and cheap and easy to understand, but it's a fairly common approach.

title: Three Food Buttons
new_elements: FoodGroupButtons (Three picture buttons for common food groups.); OneTouchFoodGroup (Starts an appropriate cycle for that group.)
rationale: Three pictures cover most foods, avoiding complex mode selection.
judge_comment: Three picture buttons are very simple and feasible, but they're limited in coverage and not radical.

title: Pull-Cord Start
new_elements: PullCord (A simple hanging cord like a light switch.); PullToCook (Starts a safe default heating cycle.)
rationale: A single pull starts cooking and is instantly understood.
judge_comment: A pull cord is intuitive and quirky, but a default cycle ignores food differences and the cord is awkward to use on a countertop appliance.

title: Foot Pedal Start
new_elements: FootPedal (Floor pedal linked to the microwave start circuit.); HandsFreeStart (Starts cooking when stepped on.)
rationale: Stepping on a pedal starts cooking with no hand controls to learn.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is novel, but it adds an odd and potentially unsafe interaction without helping the user choose settings.

title: No Timer On/Off
new_elements: OnOffLever (A single lever replaces timer and power controls.); SimpleHeatUntilStop (Heats until manually switched off or auto-safe stop.)
rationale: It works like a light switch, so no time setting is required.
judge_comment: Light-switch style heating is simple but needs auto-safe stop and risks overheating or forgotten food, with a vague mechanism.

title: Single Power Level
new_elements: SinglePowerButton (One button replaces the five-step power knob.); FixedPowerCook (Always uses an optimal power level.)
rationale: Removing power choice leaves only one obvious action.
judge_comment: Removing power choice is easy and simplifying, but a single fixed power gives poor results for many foods.

title: Twist-Once Timer
new_elements: SpringTimer (Mechanical timer with one twist range.); OneTwistMaxFive (Twist once up to five minutes and it runs.)
rationale: A single twist to five minutes replaces an arbitrary 0-30 minute dial.
judge_comment: A mechanical spring timer with a single twist is intuitive, cheap and proven, though the five-minute limit is restrictive.

title: Big Red Start
new_elements: BigRedButton (Oversized start button with one function.); BigStartOnly (Starts a default reheating cycle.)
rationale: One oversized button is unmistakable and simple to use.
judge_comment: One big start button is very easy to use but is a familiar approach and the default cycle may not suit all foods.

title: Soft-Close Auto-Latch
new_elements: MagneticLatch (Magnetic catch replaces push-release door button.); AutoLatchNoButton (Door closes and seals without a release control.)
rationale: Door closes with a push, eliminating release-button learning.
judge_comment: A magnetic catch removes a control, but opening the door still needs a mechanism, and the benefit to operation is marginal.

title: No Door Button Push
new_elements: PushPullDoor (Door opens and closes by simple push or pull.); PushToOpenPushToClose (No separate latch or release action.)
rationale: The door works like a cabinet, so there is no latch control to learn.
judge_comment: Simplifies door operation, but the safety interlock and latch are still needed, and it is only a minor part of the learning curve.

title: Proximity Wake
new_elements: ProximitySensor (Detects a hand or body near the microwave.); WakeOnApproach (Lights only the single relevant control.)
rationale: Interface appears only when needed, reducing confusion.
judge_comment: Showing only the relevant control reduces confusion and is quite feasible, though the sensor is not really a substitution for a simpler part.

title: Transparent Body No Light
new_elements: TransparentCasing (See-through microwave shell replaces metal panels.); SeeInsideWithoutLamp (User sees food directly without interior light.)
rationale: User sees food directly and no light control exists to learn.
judge_comment: A transparent body would leak microwaves, so it is infeasible, and it barely affects operation complexity.

title: Camera Window No Light
new_elements: DoorCamera (Small camera replaces peephole and lamp.); DoorScreenView (Live view on the door surface.)
rationale: A simple live view replaces peering through holes or light controls.
judge_comment: A camera is feasible but adds cost and complexity, and the screen heats up, so it is more complicated than a lamp.

title: Wave Stirrer No Turntable
new_elements: ModeStirrer (Fixed metal stirrer spreads microwaves evenly.); EvenHeatWithoutTurntable (No rotating plate is needed.)
rationale: No turntable to align or clean, so there is one less user step.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in real microwaves and remove the turntable, which helps a little with cleaning and alignment.

title: Rotating Antenna No Turntable
new_elements: RotatingAntenna (Motorized antenna moves the microwave field.); ScanMicrowaveField (Distributes energy without a moving plate.)
rationale: Internal antenna moves, so user never handles or positions a turntable.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas (mode stirrers) exist and remove the turntable, but this has little effect on operating simplicity.

title: Fixed Shelf No Turntable
new_elements: FixedGlassShelf (Static shelf replaces rotating turntable.); StaticCookSurface (Food can be placed anywhere on the shelf.)
rationale: Just place food anywhere on the shelf, with no spinning parts to learn.
judge_comment: Flatbed microwaves already exist, and a fixed shelf mostly removes a minor annoyance rather than any learning curve.

title: Smartphone One-Tap
new_elements: PhoneAppLink (Bluetooth or Wi-Fi link to a phone app.); OneTapRemoteCook (A single app button sends the full cook cycle.)
rationale: A single phone tap does all settings, so the panel stays unused.
judge_comment: Phone apps add setup and complexity, which undercuts the zero-learning-curve goal, and many products already offer this.

title: Smart Speaker Voice
new_elements: SmartSpeakerLink (Connects to an existing voice assistant.); SpeakToCook (Voice assistant translates plain language into settings.)
rationale: The user speaks naturally, so no microwave interface must be learned.
judge_comment: Voice control is natural and needs no learning, but it requires an assistant and is already on the market.

title: Gesture Wave
new_elements: GestureSensor (Low-cost infrared gesture detector.); WaveToStart (A wave starts a default heating cycle.)
rationale: Waving a hand starts cooking without touching or reading controls.
judge_comment: Wave-to-start is intuitive, but a default cycle can't suit different foods and users may not discover the gesture.

title: Haptic Single Knob
new_elements: HapticKnob (One knob with force feedback and safe stops.); GuidedOneKnob (Guides user through only a few preset positions.)
rationale: The knob only moves through safe presets, giving feedback without learning.
judge_comment: A haptic knob with a few preset positions is plausible and intuitive, but force feedback adds cost and the SUBSTITUTE link is fairly loose.

title: Child-Proof One Motion
new_elements: SingleMotionDial (One deliberate turn-and-press motion.); OneMotionCook (Starts cooking with one combined action.)
rationale: One deliberate motion starts cooking, with no multi-step sequence.
judge_comment: A turn-and-press dial is easy to build and simple to use, but it doesn't say what gets cooked or for how long, so it isn't clearly zero-learning.

title: Color-Coded Food Buttons
new_elements: ColorFoodButtons (Buttons colored to match common food packages.); ColorMatchCook (User matches color rather than reading labels.)
rationale: Matching a food color to a button replaces reading and mode selection.
judge_comment: Color matching avoids reading, but food packages vary widely and the mapping to cooking parameters is unclear.

title: Reheat Only Button
new_elements: ReheatButton (One button dedicated to reheating leftovers.); ReheatPreset (Runs a safe reheating cycle automatically.)
rationale: For most use, one reheat button removes all choices.
judge_comment: Simple and feasible, but one-touch reheat buttons already exist, so it is not radical, and a single preset covers little.

title: Defrost Only Button
new_elements: DefrostButton (One button dedicated to defrosting.); DefrostPreset (Runs a safe defrost cycle automatically.)
rationale: One dedicated defrost action avoids power and time setup.
judge_comment: A dedicated defrost button is already common and very limited in scope, so it adds little for general simplicity.

title: Popcorn Only Button
new_elements: PopcornButton (One button dedicated to popcorn.); PopcornPreset (Runs the optimal popcorn cycle.)
rationale: A single-purpose button is instantly understood.
judge_comment: Popcorn buttons already exist on most microwaves, and a single-purpose button covers only one use case, so it is neither radical nor a full substitution.

title: Beverage Only Button
new_elements: BeverageButton (One button dedicated to warming drinks.); BeveragePreset (Runs a safe beverage warming cycle.)
rationale: One button warms drinks without any settings.
judge_comment: Beverage presets are common; it is easy to use but narrow and not wild.

title: Leftover Only Button
new_elements: LeftoverButton (One button named for leftovers.); LeftoverPreset (Runs an everyday reheating cycle.)
rationale: A named everyday task replaces abstract power levels.
judge_comment: A reheat button is standard, though naming it for the task is mildly helpful and not very novel.

title: Frozen Meal Only Button
new_elements: FrozenMealButton (One button for frozen meals.); FrozenMealPreset (Runs a safe frozen-meal cycle.)
rationale: A common meal category gets one-touch operation.
judge_comment: A frozen-meal preset is a familiar feature, and the weight and variety of meals make a fixed cycle unreliable.

title: Temperature Probe Auto
new_elements: TempProbe (Simple food probe plugged into the cavity.); ProbeAutoStop (Stops cooking at a safe internal temperature.)
rationale: Insert probe and press nothing else; it stops at temperature.
judge_comment: A probe that auto-stops at a safe temperature removes time and power decisions and is the most meaningful idea here, but probes exist and add a plug-in step.

title: Humidity Auto
new_elements: HumiditySensor (Cheap sensor detects moisture in the cavity.); HumidityAutoStop (Stops cooking when moisture indicates doneness.)
rationale: Sensor detects doneness, removing timer guessing.
judge_comment: Humidity sensors already exist in sensor-cook microwaves, so this is plausible and genuinely removes timer guessing, but it is not radical.

title: Weight Auto
new_elements: ScaleBase (Built-in scale under the microwave floor.); ScaleAutoProgram (Sets a cycle from the food's weight.)
rationale: Weight on the base automatically sets the cycle.
judge_comment: A built-in scale is feasible, but weight alone does not identify the food or the right cycle, and it adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper.

title: RFID Auto
new_elements: RFIDReader (Reads passive tags on food containers.); RFIDAutoCook (Runs the correct cycle for the tagged food.)
rationale: Tagged food is recognized and cooked without any input.
judge_comment: It would be zero-input, but it needs tags on all food, which makes ecosystem adoption impractical.

title: NFC Recipe Tag
new_elements: NFCTag (Cheap sticker tag attached to recipes or containers.); TagAutoCook (Touching tag transfers cooking settings.)
rationale: Touching a recipe tag transfers settings invisibly.
judge_comment: NFC tags are cheap and workable, but users must still touch a tag, so the interaction is not fully invisible, and it mostly depends on tagged content.

title: Bluetooth Beacon Auto
new_elements: BeaconReceiver (Detects a small kitchen beacon on food packages.); BeaconAutoPreset (Presets the microwave when tagged food is near.)
rationale: Kitchen beacon tells the microwave what is being cooked, so no input is needed.
judge_comment: Proximity beacons are unreliable at identifying which item is being cooked, and the setup adds complexity that undercuts the no-learning-curve goal.

title: Motion Sensor Auto
new_elements: MotionSensor (Detects when a user steps away after placing food.); MotionAutoStart (Starts a default cycle after door closes and user moves away.)
rationale: Placing food and stepping back starts cooking automatically.
judge_comment: Auto-start when the user steps away removes all controls, but a default cycle may not suit every food and a motion sensor could trigger by mistake.

title: Sound Sensor Clap
new_elements: SoundTrigger (Simple clap or tap detector.); ClapToCook (A clap starts a default heating cycle.)
rationale: A clap starts cooking without touching or reading any control.
judge_comment: A clap is easy to learn, but ambient noise causes false triggers, a default cycle is inflexible, and it is not discoverable without being told.

title: Pressure Pad Start
new_elements: PressurePad (Pad senses when food is placed on it.); WeightPresenceStart (Starts cooking once food is present and door closes.)
rationale: Setting food on the pad and closing the door begins cooking.
judge_comment: A pressure pad is intuitive, but a weight sensor inside a microwave cavity is hard to build and clean, and the unit may start cooking empty or unsafe items.

title: Drawer Auto-Close
new_elements: AutoDrawer (Drawer mechanism replaces hinged door.); DrawerSimplePush (Push drawer closed and it starts cooking.)
rationale: Push drawer closed and it cooks, like a simple trash drawer.
judge_comment: A push-to-close drawer that starts cooking is simple and fairly radical, though it requires a mechanical redesign and spill-prone drawer sealing.

title: Clamshell One-Hand
new_elements: ClamshellDoor (Top-opening clamshell replaces side-hinged door.); OneHandCloseCook (Closing shell with one hand starts a safe default cycle.)
rationale: Closing the shell with one hand starts cooking, with no separate controls.
judge_comment: Closing the clamshell to start cooking is intuitive and mechanically plausible, though a single default cycle limits flexibility.

title: One-Touch Auto Cook
new_elements: One-Touch Cook Button (Single large button that starts a standard reheat-cook cycle.); Auto-duration and power cooking (Chooses time and power automatically for common foods.)
rationale: Removes two knobs and all timing/power decisions, so elderly users just press once.
judge_comment: Highly usable but already common on existing microwaves, and a single preset is not truly radical.

title: Pictographic Food Dial
new_elements: Pictographic Food Dial (Dial marked with pictures of tea, soup, leftovers, frozen meal.); Select food icon and start (One turn selects a complete cook program.)
rationale: Replaces abstract numbers and power levels with familiar food pictures, eliminating the learning curve.
judge_comment: Pictorial dial is intuitive and cheap, a sensible substitution of numbers with icons, though not very wild.

title: Voice Command Module
new_elements: Voice Command Module (Microphone and speech recognizer for simple spoken commands.); Natural-language cook setting (Understands phrases like 'heat my coffee'.)
rationale: Users simply say what they want instead of learning knob positions or timings.
judge_comment: Voice control is natural for users but exists already, adds cost, and the microwave still needs to know the food type.

title: RFID Food Tag Reader
new_elements: RFID/NFC Reader (Reads tags on food packages or reusable stickers.); RFID cook parameter lookup (Maps tag ID to ideal time and power.); Auto-set duration and power (No user input needed beyond placing food inside.)
rationale: Food itself tells the microwave how to cook, so the user only opens and closes the door.
judge_comment: Food tags enable zero-input cooking and are fairly novel, but they need ecosystem support and tagged packaging.

title: Weight-Sensing Auto Cook
new_elements: Cavity Weight Sensor (Weighs food placed on the turntable.); Auto-cook by weight (Calculates time and power from weight and food category.)
rationale: No need to estimate time or power; the microwave weighs the food and does the rest.
judge_comment: Weight sensing reduces guessing but still needs a food category, and it adds hardware cost rather than simplifying it.

title: Barcode Scanner
new_elements: Barcode Scanner (Internal scanner reads package barcodes.); Scan-to-cook (Looks up product cooking instructions automatically.)
rationale: Users scan the package and press start, with no manual programming.
judge_comment: Scan-and-start removes manual programming, but it needs a barcode database and it only works for packaged foods.

title: Camera AI Meal Recognition
new_elements: Camera + AI Vision (Camera identifies food type and quantity.); Recognize food and auto-cook (Chooses a safe cooking profile automatically.)
rationale: The microwave sees the food and decides everything, so operation is just place-and-close.
judge_comment: Place-and-close operation fits the need very well, but reliably recognizing food and judging safety is hard, and the idea is already known.

title: Humidity Doneness Sensor
new_elements: Humidity Sensor (Detects moisture released as food heats.); Stop when food is done (Ends cooking based on moisture signature.)
rationale: Removes the need to set a time; the microwave stops automatically when food is ready.
judge_comment: Sensor cooking already exists in some microwaves and it removes the need to set a time, so it is practical but not radical.

title: Single Popcorn Button
new_elements: Popcorn Preset Button (One dedicated button for popcorn.); One-press popcorn cycle (Uses a fixed optimal popcorn profile.)
rationale: A single labeled button replaces all knob settings for a common snack.
judge_comment: Popcorn buttons are already standard and the idea covers only one use case, though it is trivially simple to use.

title: Drawer Microwave No Door Button
new_elements: Pull-out Drawer Cavity (Microwave cavity slides out like a drawer.); Push-pull access (Open and close by pulling or pushing the drawer.)
rationale: Eliminates the door-release button and hinged-door motion for a familiar drawer action.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar action and is novel for a microwave, but it does not simplify the actual cooking controls and it makes spills and mechanics harder.

title: Magnetic Soft-Open Door
new_elements: Magnetic Door Seal (Magnetic gasket holds door shut without a latch button.); Pull-open access (Door opens with a gentle pull.)
rationale: Users just pull the door; no separate release button must be learned.
judge_comment: Removes the release button, but magnetic seals must meet door-interlock safety standards and the benefit to learning is modest.

title: Foot Pedal Door Release
new_elements: Foot Pedal Release (Floor pedal mechanically unlatches the door.); Hands-free door opening (Tap pedal to open door.)
rationale: Elderly users can open the door without bending or hunting for a button.
judge_comment: Mechanically simple, but a floor pedal is an extra thing to discover and does not make operation any simpler.

title: Proximity Auto-Open Door
new_elements: Proximity Sensor Door (Sensor detects hand near door and unlatching motor opens it.); Auto-open on approach (Door opens automatically when user reaches toward it.)
rationale: No button or handle is needed; the door anticipates the user.
judge_comment: Auto-open on approach is intuitive and radical, but accidental opening and the added motor and sensor raise cost and safety concerns.

title: Transparent Conductive Window
new_elements: Transparent Shielding Film (Optically clear conductive coating blocks microwaves.); Transparent EMI shielding (Metal mesh or ITO coating replaces perforated metal.); See-through monitoring (User watches food without opening the door.)
rationale: Clear viewing reduces uncertainty and the need to learn timing by trial and error.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive films are real and plausible, but better viewing only loosely relates to learning-free operation.

title: No-Lamp Transparent Cavity
new_elements: Transparent Cavity Wall (Whole cavity uses transparent shielding panels.); Transparent microwave shielding (Allows ambient light to illuminate food.); Ambient see-through cooking (No interior lamp needed for viewing.)
rationale: Users can always see inside without a lamp or window mesh, making operation more obvious.
judge_comment: A fully transparent cavity is bold, but it is hard to build, hard to keep clean, and only weakly tied to ease of operation.

title: Augmented Reality Food Window
new_elements: AR Window Overlay (Transparent display overlays cooking status on the food.); Show doneness and timer (Displays time remaining and doneness cues directly on door.)
rationale: Cooking status is shown visually without complex controls or manuals.
judge_comment: Transparent AR display shows status but does not simplify input controls, and it is costly rather than a cheaper substitute.

title: Smartphone-Controlled One Button
new_elements: Bluetooth One-Button Puck (Single physical button plus optional phone setup.); App-assisted simple cook (Phone can set favorites once, then one button cooks them.)
rationale: Complex setup can be done once by a helper, leaving only one button for daily use.
judge_comment: One physical button with one-time helper setup is highly simple, though it requires a phone for setup and is not very radical.

title: Alexa Voice Cook
new_elements: Voice Assistant Radio (Built-in assistant accepts spoken cooking commands.); Hands-free cook command (Starts cooking from a simple phrase.)
rationale: No knobs or buttons are needed; spoken commands are already familiar from home assistants.
judge_comment: Voice control is feasible and familiar, but it already exists commercially and is not radical.

title: Clap-to-Cook
new_elements: Acoustic Clap Sensor (Detects a sharp clap to start cooking.); Clap starts standard reheat (Triggers a safe default reheat cycle.)
rationale: A single clap replaces all controls, making operation intuitive and playful.
judge_comment: A clap trigger is simple, playful and cheap, but it risks false triggers and offers only a single default cycle.

title: Talk-to-It Natural Language
new_elements: Natural Language Processor (Understands full sentences about food and desired warmth.); Conversational cooking (User says what they want in their own words.)
rationale: Users do not need to learn modes; they simply describe the outcome they want.
judge_comment: Natural-language input removes the need to learn modes, but it is vague on implementation and overlaps with voice control.

title: Package QR Scan
new_elements: QR Code Scanner (Reads QR codes printed on food packaging.); Scan package instructions (Sets exact time and power from package data.)
rationale: Cooking instructions come from the package, so users do not need to interpret them.
judge_comment: Scanning package codes removes interpretation, but it depends on packaging adopting machine-readable cooking data and on an added scanner and UI.

title: Doneness-Only Control
new_elements: Doneness Dial (Dial marked from warm to well-done instead of minutes.); Cook to texture preference (Sensor feedback stops at selected doneness.)
rationale: Users choose an outcome, not a time or power setting, eliminating cooking knowledge.
judge_comment: Choosing an outcome instead of time is highly intuitive, and sensor-based doneness already exists on some units, though reliability varies.

title: Keep-Warm Single Mode
new_elements: Keep-Warm Toggle (Single switch for a gentle keep-warm cycle.); Single keep-warm power (Fixed low duty cycle for warming without overcooking.)
rationale: One switch replaces the five-step power knob for the most common gentle-heat need.
judge_comment: It is simple and easy to build, but it covers only a narrow use case and does not remove learning for general cooking.

title: Reheat Single Button
new_elements: Reheat Button (Large button labeled with a plate icon.); One-touch reheat cycle (Uses a sensor-guided reheat program.)
rationale: The most common task becomes a single labeled press with no settings.
judge_comment: Reheat buttons are already common, so it is highly usable but not radical.

title: Defrost Single Button
new_elements: Defrost Button (Large button labeled with a snowflake icon.); One-touch defrost cycle (Runs a safe defrost profile automatically.)
rationale: Defrosting becomes one obvious press instead of a learned sequence.
judge_comment: A defrost button is standard on existing microwaves, so it is clear and feasible but offers little novelty.

title: Beverage Single Button
new_elements: Beverage Button (Button labeled with a cup icon.); One-touch beverage heat (Heats a standard mug without settings.)
rationale: A familiar pictogram button replaces all time and power decisions for drinks.
judge_comment: Clear one-touch drink button that removes decisions, but one-touch presets already exist on many microwaves and it is not radical.

title: Frozen Meal Single Button
new_elements: Frozen Meal Button (Button labeled with a frozen dinner icon.); One-touch frozen meal cycle (Uses a longer sensor-assisted program.)
rationale: The user presses the meal picture and walks away, with no programming.
judge_comment: Sensor-assisted frozen meal button is plausible and easy to use, but it is a common preset and doesn't truly substitute any parts.

title: Big Twist-One-Minute Knob
new_elements: Detented One-Twist Timer Knob (Each detent adds exactly one minute.); One twist equals one minute (Physical detents make time obvious by feel.)
rationale: Time is set by countable clicks, so no fine reading or learning is required.
judge_comment: A detented one-minute knob is very intuitive and cheap, replacing a keypad with a mechanical timer, though it is a retro approach.

title: Color-Changing Timer Dial
new_elements: Color-Changing Timer Dial (Dial face shifts color as time elapses.); Visual time remaining (Shows progress without numbers.)
rationale: Users see how much time is left through color rather than interpreting a clock.
judge_comment: Color shows time remaining but doesn't simplify setting the operation, so it helps little with the learning curve.

title: Braille/Tactile Control Panel
new_elements: Tactile Icon Panel (Raised icons and Braille labels on a simple panel.); Touch-only control recognition (Users identify controls by feel.)
rationale: Touch labels reduce reliance on vision and memory, helping users operate without instruction.
judge_comment: Tactile icons aid accessibility and discoverability, but they don't simplify the operation logic and are not radical.

title: Two-Button Low/High Power
new_elements: Low/High Power Rocker (Two-position rocker for low or high power.); Binary power selection (Only two clearly labeled power levels.)
rationale: Replaces five ambiguous power steps with two obvious choices.
judge_comment: Simple and easy to use, but it is a mild simplification and not radical; it still requires choosing a power level and a time.

title: Automatic Power from Weight
new_elements: Weight-Based Power Selector (Sets power automatically from load weight.); Auto power by load (No power knob needed.)
rationale: Power is chosen invisibly, so the user never has to understand duty cycles.
judge_comment: Auto power from load weight removes a decision and is plausible with a load cell, though weight is a weak proxy for food type and the idea is not very detailed.

title: Steam-Sensor Auto Stop
new_elements: Steam Sensor (Detects steam rising from food.); Auto stop at steam (Ends cooking when steam is detected.)
rationale: Users do not set a timer; the microwave stops based on food condition.
judge_comment: Steam or humidity sensors already exist in sensor-cook microwaves, so it is proven and removes the timer, though it is not very novel.

title: Thermal Probe Auto Stop
new_elements: Thermal Probe (Probe measures internal food temperature.); Auto stop at target temp (Stops when food reaches selected temperature.)
rationale: Cooking becomes automatic once a simple target temperature is chosen.
judge_comment: Probe cooking exists, but inserting a probe and choosing a target temperature adds steps and a learning burden.

title: RFID Disposable Food Sticker
new_elements: Disposable RFID Sticker (Sticker placed on food container carries cooking data.); Food-specific cook instructions (Microwave reads sticker and cooks automatically.)
rationale: The sticker carries the recipe, so users do not need to remember settings.
judge_comment: A sticker that carries the recipe makes operation nearly zero-learning and is fairly novel, but it depends on food packaging adoption and a reader in the microwave.

title: Smart Plate With NFC
new_elements: NFC Smart Plate (Plate stores cooking preferences and food type.); Plate tells microwave how to cook (Microwave reads plate and starts correct cycle.)
rationale: The everyday act of putting food on a plate automatically configures cooking.
judge_comment: A plate that configures the cook cycle removes nearly all operation steps, though it needs special plates and the NFC-stored cooking data is loosely defined.

title: No-Turntable Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Mode Stirrer (Fixed rotating stirrer distributes microwaves evenly.); Even heating without turntable alignment (No need to center or align food.)
rationale: Users do not have to learn turntable placement or alignment.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in real microwaves, and removing the turntable's alignment need helps only modestly with operation simplicity.

title: Drawer with Auto-Close
new_elements: Auto-Close Drawer (Drawer gently self-closes after a push.); Gentle self-close access (No latch button or hard push needed.)
rationale: A familiar soft-close drawer action removes the door-button learning step.
judge_comment: A soft-close drawer is feasible and familiar, but it only marginally reduces learning since opening and closing a door is already simple.

title: Kick-to-Open Door
new_elements: Kick Sensor (Detects a gentle kick or foot tap on lower panel.); Foot-tap door opening (Opens door without using hands.)
rationale: Opening the microwave becomes a natural foot tap, requiring no button instruction.
judge_comment: Foot-tap opening is quirky and could trigger accidentally, and it is arguably less discoverable than a button.

title: Wave-to-Open Door
new_elements: Gesture Sensor Door (Infrared gesture sensor detects a wave.); Wave to open (Door opens with a hand wave.)
rationale: No physical button must be found or pressed; a wave is universally understood.
judge_comment: Wave-to-open is plausible with an IR sensor, but it only addresses opening and is not self-evidently intuitive, so it adds little for the cooking steps.

title: Face-Recognition Auto-Start
new_elements: Face Recognition Camera (Recognizes household member and their favorite preset.); Recognize user and favorite cook (Starts the user's usual cycle automatically.)
rationale: The microwave remembers personal presets so the user does nothing but stand nearby.
judge_comment: Zero-interaction start is highly relevant and novel, but a camera in a kitchen appliance raises privacy and cost concerns, and auto-starting without confirming the food is a safety risk.

title: One-Touch Leftovers Button
new_elements: Leftovers Button (Button labeled with a leftover container icon.); Auto reheat leftovers (Sensor guesses safe reheat cycle.)
rationale: A common use case is reduced to one clearly labeled press.
judge_comment: A single labeled button is simple and practical, but similar buttons already exist and the sensor is vaguely specified.

title: One-Touch Mug Cake Button
new_elements: Mug Cake Button (Button labeled with a mug cake icon.); Auto dessert cycle (Runs a precise short dessert program.)
rationale: Specific popular recipes become one-press operations with no timing knowledge.
judge_comment: Easy to build, but it serves a narrow use case and is a standard preset button, so it is neither radical nor broadly relevant.

title: Single Rotary Cook Dial
new_elements: Single Rotary Cook Dial (One dial sets a complete cooking program.); Turn to set time and power together (Internal linkage maps dial position to time and power.)
rationale: Two confusing knobs are replaced by one dial with a single motion.
judge_comment: A single dial is simple and feasible, but it is a modest change and mapping time to power in one motion could confuse users.

title: Snap-On Cooking Capsule
new_elements: Snap-On Recipe Capsule (Physical capsule keyed to a recipe program.); Preloaded cook program (Insert capsule and press start.)
rationale: Users choose a physical recipe capsule instead of entering any settings.
judge_comment: A physical keyed capsule is intuitive and fairly novel, but it needs a capsule ecosystem and adds ongoing cost.

title: QR Code on Appliance Itself
new_elements: Self-QR Help Overlay (Large QR code links to a 30-second how-to video.); Show video on phone (User scans code to see simple instructions.)
rationale: In-the-moment video help removes the need to read a manual or remember controls.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap, but it requires a phone and a video, so it adds a step instead of removing the learning curve.

title: Talking Microwave Announces Settings
new_elements: Voice Feedback Speaker (Speaks selected time, power, and completion.); Speaks selected time and power (Confirms settings verbally.)
rationale: Spoken confirmation reduces uncertainty and makes knob effects obvious without learning.
judge_comment: Voice confirmation helps clarity and is easy to build, but talking appliances already exist and it is not radical.

title: Haptic Confirmation Knob
new_elements: Haptic Knob (Knob vibrates at common presets.); Vibrates at presets (Physical feedback guides users to common settings.)
rationale: Users feel when they reach useful presets, so they do not need to learn exact positions.
judge_comment: Detents and haptics help users find presets, but they do little for first-time understanding and the haptic motor adds cost.

title: Single Button with Long-Press Power Selection
new_elements: Long-Press Multi-Function Button (Short press cooks; long press cycles power.); Short press cook, long press power (One button handles both primary settings.)
rationale: A single button with one optional long-press replaces both knobs with minimal learning.
judge_comment: A single button is simple and cheap, but the long-press needs to be learned and is hidden.

title: Auto-Cook on Door Close
new_elements: Door-Close Auto-Cook Sensor (Detects when door is closed with food inside.); Starts standard cycle automatically (Runs a safe default reheat after door close.)
rationale: The microwave starts itself when the door closes, so there are no controls to learn at all.
judge_comment: It removes controls entirely, which is radical, but starting a cycle with no user intent is risky (empty or unsuitable items, metal) and needs safety sensing.

title: One-Button Cook
new_elements: Single cook button (Replaces timer and power knobs with one start control.); Auto-select cooking profile (Infers time and power from food category or defaults.)
rationale: Removes all timer and power decisions so first-time users just press once.
judge_comment: Highly simple and plausible, but a one-button auto-profile is a familiar idea and the inference mechanism is vague.

title: RFID Meal Tags
new_elements: NFC recipe tag (Sticker or tray tag that stores cook settings.); NFC reader (Reads the tag and sets time and power automatically.); Auto-set cook cycle (Loads correct time and power without user input.)
rationale: Food itself carries the settings, so the user never learns the panel.
judge_comment: NFC tags are plausible and concrete, but they require tagged food or an ecosystem, and the idea is not a true substitution of a cheaper part.

title: Barcode Scan-to-Cook
new_elements: Barcode scanner (Scans packaged food barcodes inside or outside the cavity.); Lookup cook program (Matches barcode to an automatic cooking program.)
rationale: Scanning is a familiar zero-learning action that replaces manual programming.
judge_comment: Barcode lookup is workable and familiar, but it needs a database and scanning adds a step, and it does not cover unpackaged food.

title: Weight-Sensing Auto-Time
new_elements: Cavity weight sensor (Measures food mass on the turntable.); Mass-to-time calculation (Sets cook duration from weight automatically.)
rationale: The microwave figures out time from weight, so no timer knowledge is needed.
judge_comment: A load cell under the turntable is feasible and removes timer decisions, though weight alone does not determine food type or power.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity sensor (Detects steam release from food.); Steam-based doneness stop (Stops cooking when food reaches doneness.)
rationale: User only presses start; the microwave decides when food is done.
judge_comment: Humidity sensing for auto-stop already exists in sensor-cook models, but it fits the one-press need very well.

title: Infrared Doneness Auto-Stop
new_elements: IR surface thermometer (Non-contact temperature sensor aimed at food surface.); Target-temperature stop (Stops cooking at a safe preset surface temperature.)
rationale: No time or power setting is required; cooking ends by temperature.
judge_comment: An IR sensor that stops at a target temperature removes time and power settings, but it reads only surface temperature, which is unreliable for microwave heating and does not detect the food type.

title: Acoustic Doneness Sensor
new_elements: MEMS microphone array (Listens to popping, bubbling, and sizzling sounds.); Sound-based doneness detection (Infers when food is cooked from acoustic signature.)
rationale: The appliance listens for done-ness so the user does not need to set anything.
judge_comment: Listening for doneness would make operation truly zero-input and is highly novel, but noise from the fan and turntable plus the many silent foods make it hard to do reliably.

title: More/Less Simple Dial
new_elements: More-less rocker (Two-button rocker replaces full timer and power knobs.); Relative adjustment (Adjusts an auto-cook result up or down after the fact.)
rationale: Users only learn more or less, not minutes or power levels.
judge_comment: A more/less rocker is simple and easy to build, but it is incremental and only works if the auto-cook result is already good.

title: Food-Icon Dial
new_elements: Icon dial (Rotary dial with food pictograms instead of numbers.); Picture-based program selection (Selects a cook program by recognizable food image.)
rationale: Pictures eliminate text and timer learning.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial is intuitive and cheap, though it is a familiar approach and offers limited accuracy for different portions.

title: Gentle/Normal/Boost Slider
new_elements: Three-position sliders (Replaces five-step power cam with gentle, normal, boost.); Simplified power selection (Maps complex duty cycles to three intuitive choices.)
rationale: Three words are easier than five numbered power steps.
judge_comment: A three-position power slider is easy to understand and build, but users still have to choose a time, so it only partly removes the learning curve.

title: Twist Egg Timer Substitute
new_elements: Spring egg timer (Cheap mechanical twist timer with one intuitive gesture.); Gesture-based duration (Twist amount maps directly to time without reading.)
rationale: Twisting an egg timer is universally understood and needs no display.
judge_comment: A mechanical twist timer is a very intuitive, cheap input that directly removes the learning curve, though it is a familiar design (older microwaves used it).

title: Light Ring Instead of Bell
new_elements: Completion light ring (Colored LED ring replaces mechanical bell.); Visual done signal (Signals completion without a startling sound.)
rationale: A light is instantly understood and needs no audio learning.
judge_comment: A light ring is easy to understand, but it only covers the done signal and may be missed when the user is out of view.

title: Phone Notification Instead of Bell
new_elements: Bluetooth completion beacon (Sends done alert to phone.); Remote done notification (User gets a familiar phone buzz instead of a bell.)
rationale: Uses an already-learned notification pattern instead of appliance-specific bell.
judge_comment: A phone alert adds pairing and setup, which works against the no-learning-curve goal, and it is not very radical.

title: Push-to-Open Door
new_elements: Push-to-open latch (Door opens by pressing the door itself, replacing release button.); Whole-door release (Any push on the door edge opens it.)
rationale: No separate button to find; the door itself is the control.
judge_comment: Push-to-open removes the need to find a button and is simple and proven, though it only touches door opening.

title: Foot-Pedal Door Release
new_elements: Foot pedal release (Low pedal opens door without hands.); Hands-free door opening (Kicks door open for messy hands.)
rationale: A pedal is a simple, obvious substitute for a small push button.
judge_comment: A foot pedal is unusual and hands-free, but it is not obvious to users and adds hardware, so it does little for simplicity.

title: Full-Door Press Latch
new_elements: Full-edge press latch (Whole door edge is a compliant release surface.); Press-anywhere release (User can press anywhere along the door edge.)
rationale: Eliminates the need to locate a small door button.
judge_comment: A full-edge press latch makes opening easier, but the door button was never the main learning-curve problem and the idea is incremental.

title: Magnetic Reed Interlock
new_elements: Magnetic reed safety interlock (Contactless reed switches replace mechanical microswitches.); Door-closed detection (Detects door state with no moving actuator.)
rationale: Removes complicated mechanical interlock feel so the door just works.
judge_comment: Reed switches are an internal safety swap that users never notice, and their safety certification is a concern, so the link to simple operation is weak.

title: RFID Door Presence Interlock
new_elements: RFID door presence tag (Passive tag in door frame confirms door position.); Contactless safety check (Prevents operation unless door tag is present.)
rationale: No mechanical interlock learning or force needed to close safely.
